plain: When you ask Claude to review code or flag problems, it only knows what counts as a problem if you tell it. Saying "be careful" or "only report what you are sure of" does not help much. Listing exactly which kinds of issue to report, and which to ignore, is what cuts down false alarms. A false positive is a finding that turns out not to be a real problem.
analogy: Telling a new proofreader "be careful" gets you a page covered in red ink. Telling them "mark spelling errors and wrong dates, ignore comma style" gets you the five marks you actually need.

sections.body:
**Precision comes from telling Claude exactly what counts, not from asking it to be careful.**

Precision is the share of flagged items that are real problems. If a review bot posts 30 comments and only 3 matter, precision is 10%. The other 27 are **false positives**: alarms that turn out not to be problems.

Claude cannot guess your bar. Compare:

- Vague: "check that comments are accurate".
- Specific: "flag a comment only when its claimed behaviour contradicts the code".

The vague version lets Claude flag any comment that is slightly loose. The specific version gives it a yes/no test it can apply to each comment. Explicit **categorical criteria** like this are what raise precision.

sections.h: How to write report and skip lists
sections.body:
**Write two lists, what to report and what to skip, then define each severity level with code.**

Step by step:

1. **Report list.** Name concrete categories: behaviour bugs, security issues such as unescaped input in SQL, comments that contradict the code.
2. **Skip list.** Name the usual noise: style, naming preferences, patterns used consistently elsewhere in the repo.
3. **Severity levels.** For each of `critical`, `major` and `minor`, write the criteria and add a short code example. "Critical: serious issue" is too thin, and two runs will label the same bug differently.
4. **Test on real diffs.** Count findings per category and see where the noise comes from.

The skip list matters as much as the report list. It removes noise at the source, instead of hoping Claude filters it.

**"Be conservative" and "only report high-confidence findings" do not improve precision.**

These instructions sound sensible, but they do not change what Claude treats as a problem. If Claude believes a loosely worded comment is "inaccurate", it can be highly confident about that and still report it.

A confidence instruction:

- leaves the definition of a problem unchanged;
- often cuts some real findings along with the noise;
- adds a "high confidence" label that developers soon ignore.

What works is replacing the threshold with categories: "Report behaviour bugs. Skip comment wording that still describes the code correctly." Now Claude has a rule to apply.

Also avoid jumping to new infrastructure, such as a classifier or a three-judge vote. Those judges lack criteria too. Writing the criteria is the proportionate first fix.

**Noise in one category erodes trust in every category, so pause it while you fix it.**

Developers do not read findings category by category. If "comment accuracy" findings are wrong half the time, people start skimming the whole bot, and a real SQL injection at position 18 goes unread.

The proportionate response:

- **Disable the noisy category temporarily.** The rest of the review regains trust straight away.
- **Rewrite its criteria** with report/skip rules and examples.
- **Re-enable it** once it is reliable on a sample of real pull requests.

When not to do this: if the noise is spread across every category, the whole prompt needs explicit criteria, not one switch.

A common wrong instinct is "keep it on, its true positives are valuable". That value is lost if nobody reads the findings.

diagram.title: Two ways to cut false positives

example.title: Worked example: a review prompt with report/skip criteria
example.code:
## What to report
- Bugs: logic that changes behaviour in a way the PR does not intend.
- Security: unescaped user input in SQL, HTML or shell commands.
- Comment drift: flag a comment ONLY when its claimed behaviour
  contradicts what the code does.

## What to skip
- Style, formatting and naming preferences.
- Patterns used consistently elsewhere in this repo.
- Missing comments (absence is not a finding).

## Severity
- critical: exploitable or data-losing. Example:
  `db.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=" + req.id)`
- major: wrong result on a normal input. Example:
  `for i in range(1, len(items))`  # skips the first item
- minor: wrong result only on rare edge cases. Example:
  `avg = total / count`  # fails when count is 0 on empty export
notes: The "What to report" list names concrete categories instead of asking Claude to be careful.
The comment rule is a test Claude can apply: does the comment contradict the code, yes or no.
The "What to skip" list is just as important; it removes the usual sources of noise.
Each severity level has a code example, so labels stay consistent across runs.
There is no confidence threshold anywhere in the prompt.

labs.title: Review bot noise makes developers ignore everything
labs.context: Your CI review bot posts about 30 comments per PR, and developers now ignore all of them, including real security findings. Most of the noise comes from the comment-accuracy category, and rewriting that category's criteria will take about two weeks.
labs.question: What should the team do first to restore trust in the bot?

options.text: Add an instruction to every category to be conservative and report only findings the model is highly confident about.
options.code:
Review this diff for bugs, security issues and
inaccurate comments.

Be conservative. Only report findings you are
highly confident about.

trace.text: PR #482 opened. Review bot runs with the updated prompt.
Reviews diff. Still treats any slightly imprecise comment as "inaccurate".
Posts 26 findings, each described as high confidence.
Developer dismisses the first 10 comment-wording findings and stops reading.
A real SQL injection finding at position 18 goes unread.

options.verdict: Noise barely drops and the real bug is still missed.
options.why: Confidence instructions do not change what Claude counts as a problem, so comment-wording noise stays. Trap: a vague confidence filter where explicit criteria are needed.

options.text: Keep the prompt and add a consensus layer, where three judge calls vote on each finding before it is posted.
options.code:
findings = review(diff)  # same vague prompt
kept = []
for f in findings:
    votes = [judge(f) for _ in range(3)]
    if votes.count("real") >= 2:
        kept.append(f)
post(kept)

trace.text: Review runs with the original vague prompt: 28 findings.
Each finding sent to 3 judge calls: 84 extra API calls.
Judges also lack criteria and disagree on comment-wording findings.
Posts 14 findings. Review now takes 4 minutes longer.
Developer still sees half noise and keeps ignoring the bot.

options.verdict: Some noise removed at high cost; developers still ignore the bot.
options.why: Over-engineered: new infrastructure before the proportionate fix of explicit criteria. The judges have no criteria either, so they disagree on the same noisy findings.

options.text: Define report and skip categories, and disable the comment-accuracy category until its criteria are rewritten.
options.code:
Report: behaviour bugs; security issues
(unescaped input in SQL/HTML/shell).
Skip: style, naming, patterns used elsewhere
in this repo.

# comment-accuracy category: DISABLED while
# its criteria are rewritten

trace.text: PR #482 opened. Bot runs with report/skip lists; comment category is off.
Checks each change against the report list. Skips naming and style.
Posts 3 findings: 1 critical SQL injection, 2 major logic bugs.
Developer reads all 3 and fixes the SQL injection before merge.
Team drafts a new rule: flag comments only when they contradict the code.

options.verdict: Three real findings, all read and acted on.
options.why: False positives in one category erode trust in every category, so pausing the noisy one restores trust now. Explicit report/skip categories keep the rest precise while the criteria are rewritten.

options.text: Keep comment-accuracy running because some findings are real, and tag every finding with a severity so developers can sort them.
options.code:
Review this diff for bugs, security issues and
inaccurate comments.

Tag every finding: [critical] [major] [minor]

# comment-accuracy: ENABLED
# (it does catch some real drift)

trace.text: PR #482 opened. Bot runs with severity tags; all categories on.
Posts 27 findings: 19 are [minor] comment-wording remarks.
Developer sees the usual wall of comments and collapses them all.
The one [critical] SQL injection finding goes unread.

options.verdict: Findings are labelled, but the noise and the distrust remain.
options.why: A noisy category left running erodes trust in all categories, including the useful ones. Severity tags sort the noise but do not remove it (right pattern, wrong problem).

labs.takeaway: One noisy category poisons trust in all of them: disable it while you rewrite its criteria.

labs.title: Defect severity flips between near-identical reports
labs.context: Your pipeline extracts defect reports from warranty claims into records with a severity of critical, major or minor, and every critical record triggers a recall review. Each level is defined in one sentence, and near-identical battery-swelling reports come out critical on some runs and minor on others.
labs.question: Which change most improves the consistency of the severity field?

options.text: Rewrite each level as explicit criteria, with two or three concrete example reports per level showing where the boundaries fall.
options.code:
critical: any risk of fire, burns or injury.
  e.g. "battery swelled, casing split"
  e.g. "charger sparked at the socket"
major: product unusable, no safety risk.
  e.g. "screen dead after two days"
minor: cosmetic, still fully usable.
  e.g. "scratch on the lid on arrival"
Any battery swelling counts as critical.

trace.text: Runs 400 warranty claims through the updated prompt.
"Battery bulging, lid will not close" matches the swelling rule: critical.
"Hinge slightly loose" matches the cosmetic example: minor.
Second run on the same 400 claims: 397 labels identical.
Recall queue now holds only safety cases.

options.verdict: Same report, same label, run after run.
options.why: Per-level criteria with concrete examples show exactly where each boundary sits. One-line definitions leave the boundary to the model's judgement on every run.

options.text: Add a severity_confidence field to the schema and send any record scored below 0.8 to a human reviewer.

trace.text: Run 1: swelling report labelled critical, confidence 0.9.
Run 2: same report labelled minor, confidence 0.85.
Neither run falls below 0.8; nothing is routed.
Label still flips on 17% of borderline reports.

options.verdict: The model is confidently inconsistent.
options.why: A confidence score does not sharpen vague criteria; the model rates both answers highly. Trap: confidence-based filtering where explicit criteria are needed.

options.text: Expand each one-sentence definition into a detailed paragraph describing the factors that make a defect more or less serious.
options.code:
critical: a defect that is serious, taking into
account the likelihood of harm, the number of
users affected, the product category and any
regulatory considerations...
major: a defect of moderate seriousness...

trace.text: Runs the same 400 claims with the longer definitions.
Weighs "likelihood of harm" for slight swelling differently each run.
Labels still flip on 14% of borderline reports.

options.verdict: Longer text, same inconsistency.
options.why: More prose still leaves the boundary abstract, so borderline cases keep flipping. The rule is explicit criteria anchored by concrete examples per level.

options.text: Run the extraction three times per claim and keep whichever severity label appears in at least two of the runs.
options.code:
extraction:
  runs_per_claim: 3
  severity: majority_vote
  prompt: prompts/defects.md   # unchanged

trace.text: Each claim extracted three times: 1,200 calls instead of 400.
Borderline swelling report: critical, minor, critical.
Next day the same report votes minor, minor, critical.
Cost tripled; borderline labels still differ between days.

options.verdict: Triple the cost and the boundary is still unclear.
options.why: Over-engineered: voting averages noise from unclear criteria instead of removing it. The proportionate fix is explicit criteria with examples.

labs.takeaway: Inconsistent severity labels → explicit per-level criteria with concrete examples, not confidence scores or votes.

labs.title: Fraud flags fire on a third of refunds
labs.context: Your support agent escalates a refund to the fraud team whenever the request "might be fraudulent". It now flags 31% of refunds, mostly loyal repeat customers and large orders, and the fraud team has started clearing the queue unread. The fraud team can name the specific patterns that actually matter.
labs.question: What change most improves the precision of the fraud flags?

options.text: Add "only flag requests you are highly confident are fraudulent" to the agent's system prompt.
options.code:
Escalate to the fraud team if a refund request
might be fraudulent.

Only flag requests you are highly confident
are fraudulent.

trace.text: Agent runs on 500 refund requests.
Still reads "large order from a frequent buyer" as suspicious.
Flags drop from 31% to 26%, each marked high confidence.
Fraud team keeps clearing the queue without reading it.

options.verdict: Slightly fewer flags, same wrong ones.
options.why: Confidence wording does not tell Claude what counts as fraud, so it stays confident about the wrong cases. Trap: a confidence threshold where categorical criteria are needed.

options.text: Add a separate fraud-scoring model that rates every refund request and forwards only those scoring above a tuned threshold.
options.code:
refund_flow:
  - agent: support_agent
  - model: fraud_scorer_v1   # new, needs labelled data
    forward_if: score > 0.72
  - queue: fraud_team

trace.text: Team spends three weeks labelling past refunds to train the scorer.
Agent still escalates 31%; scorer filters the queue to 18%.
Fraud team asks why the agent flags loyal customers at all.

options.verdict: Weeks of new infrastructure; the agent is as vague as before.
options.why: Over-engineered: a new model before the proportionate fix of naming the criteria. The agent's vague instruction is still the source of the noise.

options.text: Give the agent each customer's full order history so it has more context before deciding whether to flag.

trace.text: Calls get_customer and pulls 40 past orders for a regular buyer.
"Many recent refunds and large orders" reads as suspicious.
Flag rate rises from 31% to 34%.

options.verdict: More data, judged against the same vague test.
options.why: More context does not help when the test itself is "might be fraudulent" (right pattern, wrong problem). The agent needs named criteria to apply to that context.

options.text: Replace "might be fraudulent" with named flag patterns, such as new accounts with large refunds, and named skip cases.
options.code:
Flag for fraud review ONLY when:
- account is under 14 days old AND refund > $300
- 3+ refunds to different cards in 30 days
- signed-for delivery, item claimed missing
Do NOT flag: repeat customers with normal
history, large orders alone, angry tone.

trace.text: Agent runs on the same 500 refund requests.
Repeat buyer, large order: matches a skip case, refund processed.
Account 3 days old, $640 refund: matches a flag rule, escalated.
Flag rate falls from 31% to 4%.
Fraud team reviews every flag and confirms 2 real fraud cases.

options.verdict: Few flags, all worth reading.
options.why: Specific categorical criteria tell Claude exactly what qualifies and what to ignore. That is what raises precision, not asking it to be careful.

labs.takeaway: Vague "might be X" instructions → name the categories to flag and the cases to skip.

checks.q: Why does "only report high-confidence findings" not fix false positives?
checks.a: It does not tell Claude what counts as a problem. Explicit report and skip categories do, so they are what improve precision.

checks.q: One review category is very noisy but sometimes finds real issues. What do you do?
checks.a: Disable it temporarily so its noise stops eroding trust in every category, then rewrite its criteria before turning it back on.

checks.q: How do you get consistent severity labels?
checks.a: Give explicit criteria for each level with concrete code examples, not one-line definitions.

quiz.q: A CI review bot produces many false positives. Which prompt change most directly improves precision?
options: Add "only report findings you are highly confident about".
Add a second model that votes on each finding first.
List the categories to report and the ones to skip.
Tell Claude to be conservative with borderline issues.
quiz.why: Precision comes from explicit report/skip categories. Confidence wording does not change what Claude counts as a problem, and a voting layer is over-engineered as a first fix.

quiz.q: The "comment accuracy" category is wrong about half the time but sometimes finds real issues. Developers now ignore the bot. What should you do first?
options: Disable that category for now and rewrite its criteria.
Keep it running because its true positives are valuable.
Lower its severity so its findings are listed last.
Ask developers to read every finding more carefully.
quiz.why: Noise in one category erodes trust in all of them. Pausing it restores trust while its criteria are fixed.

quiz.q: Two runs of the same review label one bug "major" and then "minor". Each severity level has a one-line definition. What fixes this?
options: Ask Claude to think harder before choosing a severity.
Remove severity labels from the review output.
Run the review three times and take the majority.
Give per-level criteria with a code example for each.
quiz.why: One-line definitions leave room for inconsistent labels. Explicit criteria with concrete code examples per level make classification consistent.

quiz.q: Which instruction gives Claude a test it can apply to each code comment?
options: Check that the code comments are accurate.
Flag a comment only when it contradicts the code.
Report comment problems you are sure about.
Be strict about the quality of all comments.
quiz.why: It turns a vague goal into a yes/no category Claude can check. The other options are vague or confidence-based.

misconceptions.myth: Asking Claude to be conservative reduces false positives.
misconceptions.fact: It does not change what Claude counts as a problem. Named report and skip categories do.

misconceptions.myth: A noisy category is worth keeping if it sometimes finds real bugs.
misconceptions.fact: Its noise makes developers ignore every category. Disable it temporarily and fix its criteria.

misconceptions.myth: A filter model or consensus vote is the best first fix for noise.
misconceptions.fact: It adds cost, and the judges have no criteria either. Explicit criteria are the proportionate first step.

scenario.title: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
scenario.story:
A payments team added a Claude review step to their CI pipeline. The prompt said: "Review this diff for bugs, security issues and inaccurate comments. Be conservative."

Within two weeks the bot averaged 30 comments per pull request. Most were about comment wording, such as a docstring that said "returns a list" when the function returned a tuple. Developers began closing the bot's comments unread. One afternoon a real SQL injection finding sat at position 18 and nobody saw it.

The tech lead counted findings by category: 80% of the noise came from comment accuracy. She turned that category off. Then she rewrote the prompt with a report list (behaviour bugs, unescaped input in SQL, HTML or shell), a skip list (style, naming, patterns used elsewhere in the repo) and a code example for each severity level.

The next week the bot posted three or four findings per pull request, and developers read them all. The comment category came back later with one rule: flag a comment only when it contradicts the code.

plain: Few-shot prompting means putting a few worked examples in your prompt: an input and the exact output you want. Claude copies the format and learns where the line sits between "flag this" and "leave it". It is the go-to fix when detailed written instructions still give inconsistent results.
analogy: You can describe a filled-in tax form in three pages of rules, or you can hand someone two completed forms. The completed forms answer questions the rules never thought of.

sections.body:
**A few-shot prompt shows Claude 2 to 4 worked examples, so it can copy both the format and the judgement.**

"Few-shot" means placing a few examples of input and desired output in the prompt, before the real task. A review prompt might show one code snippet with its finding written as `location | issue | severity | fix`, then ask Claude to review the real diff.

Examples do two jobs that prose struggles with:

- **Format.** Claude sees the exact shape of a good answer, field by field.
- **Judgement.** Claude sees where the **decision boundary** sits: the line between "report this" and "this is fine".

Few-shot prompting is the most effective fix when you have already written detailed instructions and the output is still inconsistent.

**Pick examples for the hard, ambiguous cases, and show why each decision was made.**

Step by step:

1. **Find the ambiguous case.** Look at outputs that came back inconsistent. That is where examples help. The obvious case needs none.
2. **Write a contrastive pair.** Two snippets that look alike, where only one is a real issue. For example, `except Exception: pass` in a retry loop (hides failures, report it) next to `except FileNotFoundError: return None` for an optional cache (expected, skip it).
3. **Add a "Why" line** to each example, saying why that action beat the plausible alternative.
4. **Stop at 2 to 4.** Ten copies of the easy case use tokens and teach nothing about the boundary.

Examples of acceptable patterns are what cut false positives. Without them, Claude flags anything that looks like a bug.

**When fields come back empty on a new layout, add examples from varied document structures.**

In extraction, the warning sign is a required field that is null, or invented, only on certain documents. Usually Claude has not seen that layout.

Example: every example paper puts the sample size under a "Methods" heading. A conference paper says "across 48 teams (n=312)" in its introduction instead. Claude finds no Methods heading and returns null.

The fix is examples across **varied structures**:

- a journal paper with a Methods section and a reference list;
- a conference paper with inline "[Lee 2021]" citations and details in prose;
- a position paper with no study, where `sample_size: null` is correct.

The last example matters. It shows that null is right when the data is truly absent, which reduces hallucination.

**More prose, more retries or more easy examples do not fix an unclear boundary.**

Common mistakes:

- **Expanding the instructions.** Detailed instructions are what already failed. Adding "look very carefully" rarely changes the result.
- **Only positive examples.** If every example is a real bug, Claude cannot see what acceptable code looks like, so false positives stay high.
- **Retrying the same prompt.** On a layout Claude has not seen, a retry gives the same answer. It is the right pattern for the wrong problem.
- **Near-identical examples.** Claude may copy surface details, such as a variable name, instead of the rule. Vary them so it generalises.

When not to use few-shot: if the output is already consistent, or if the real problem is data missing from the source (lesson 4.4).

example.title: Worked example: contrastive few-shot for a review bot
example.code:
Report each finding as: location | issue | severity | fix

<example>
Code: except Exception: pass   # in retry_upload()
Output: uploader.py:42 | errors swallowed, failed uploads
  look successful | major | log and re-raise after retries
Why: hides failures from the caller, not just noisy.
</example>

<example>
Code: except FileNotFoundError: return None  # in load_cache()
Output: (no finding)
Why: a missing cache is an expected state and the caller
  checks for None. Narrow catch, documented intent.
</example>

Now review the following diff:
notes: The first line fixes the output format; both examples follow it.
The two examples are a contrastive pair: both catch an exception, only one is a real issue.
Each example has a "Why" line, so Claude learns the reasoning, not just the label.
Two targeted examples cover the ambiguous case; there are none for obvious bugs.

labs.title: Fields come back null on a new layout
labs.context: Your pipeline extracts sample_size and citations from research papers. It works on journal papers, but on conference papers with inline citations and no Methods heading both fields come back null 80% of the time. The prompt already has detailed instructions on where these values can appear.
labs.question: What change most reliably fixes the null fields?

options.text: Strengthen the instructions: say the values may appear anywhere in the paper, and that required fields must never be left empty.
options.code:
Extract sample_size and citations.
IMPORTANT: sample_size may appear anywhere.
Look very carefully in all sections.
Citations may be formatted in different ways.
Never leave required fields empty.

trace.text: Runs on 50 conference papers.
Searches for a Methods heading, does not find one.
"Never leave empty" pushes it to guess: sample_size = 100 on 9 papers.
Spot check: 9 guessed values are wrong; 31 papers still null.

options.verdict: Still empty on most papers, and now some values are invented.
options.why: Detailed instructions are what already failed, and pressure to fill fields causes invented values. Trap: more prose where examples are needed.

options.text: Add a few examples from different layouts, including a conference paper with inline citations and a paper with no study.
options.code:
<example type="journal">
Methods: "We recruited 214 adults..." -> sample_size: 214
References list at end -> citations: [...]
</example>
<example type="conference">
Intro para: "...across 48 teams (n=312)" -> sample_size: 312
Inline "[Lee 2021]" -> citations: ["Lee 2021"]
</example>
<example type="no-sample">
Position paper, no study -> sample_size: null
</example>

trace.text: Runs on the same 50 conference papers.
Recognises the inline "(n=...)" pattern from the conference example.
Collects inline [Author Year] citations instead of hunting for a references list.
Null rate drops from 80% to 6%; the remaining nulls are position papers with no study.

options.verdict: Fields fill correctly and genuine nulls stay null.
options.why: Examples across varied structures show Claude where the data lives in each layout. The no-study example also shows that null is right when the data is absent.

options.text: Retry each paper that returns a null field, up to three times, and keep the first non-null result.

trace.text: 40 papers return null sample_size on first pass.
Retries each up to 3 times with the same prompt: 120 extra calls.
Same layout, same examples: same result on 37 of 40.
Cost triples; null rate barely changes.

options.verdict: Expensive and almost no improvement.
options.why: Retrying is the right pattern for the wrong problem: the model has not seen this layout. Varied-structure examples address the cause.

options.text: Add a classifier that labels each paper's layout, then route each layout to its own specialised prompt.
options.code:
pipeline:
  - step: classify_layout   # journal | conference | other
  - step: extract
    prompt_by_layout:
      journal: prompts/journal.md
      conference: prompts/conference.md  # new prose
      other: prompts/journal.md

trace.text: Classifier labels workshop papers as "other": they get the journal prompt.
Conference prompt is new prose with no examples; still looks for Methods.
Null rate drops from 80% to 61%.
Team now maintains three prompts and a classifier.

options.verdict: New infrastructure, still mostly null.
options.why: Over-engineered: a routing layer before the proportionate fix. Each route is still prose instructions, which is what already failed.

labs.takeaway: Nulls on an unfamiliar layout → examples across varied structures, including a genuine-null case.

labs.title: Reviewer flags every deliberate catch-all handler
labs.context: Your CI reviewer flags error handling that swallows exceptions and catches real bugs, but it also flags the repository's top-level request handlers, which deliberately catch everything and log it. 40% of its error-handling comments are dismissed, and a detailed paragraph explaining the difference is already in the prompt. The team wants fewer dismissals without losing the real catches.
labs.question: What is the most effective next step?

options.text: Add six more examples of genuinely swallowed exceptions, each showing location, issue, severity and suggested fix.
options.code:
<example>
billing/charge.py:42  except Exception: pass
Issue: failure hidden from caller
Severity: major
Fix: log and re-raise
</example>
... five more real issues, same shape ...

trace.text: PR #610 reviewed with six new issue examples.
Output format is perfect: location, issue, severity, fix.
Flags handlers/api.py catch-all again as "swallowed exception".
Dismissal rate on error-handling comments: 39%.

options.verdict: Nicely formatted, still wrong about the handlers.
options.why: Examples of real issues only leave the decision boundary unclear. Without an acceptable-pattern example, the false positives stay.

options.text: Disable the error-handling category until the prompt is rewritten, because its false positives erode trust in the bot.
options.code:
review_categories:
  security: on
  bugs: on
  error_handling: off   # until prompt fixed

trace.text: Error-handling category switched off.
PR #614 merges with "except Exception: pass" around a payment call.
Failed charges are silently marked as paid in production.

options.verdict: No false positives, and no real catches either.
options.why: Disabling suits a category developers already ignore; here they still read it and the real catches matter. The prompt has already been rewritten once, so the next step is a better fix, not a pause.

options.text: Expand the paragraph into a full procedure listing every file and function where a catch-all handler is allowed.
options.code:
Catch-all handlers are acceptable ONLY in:
- handlers/api.py: handle_request
- handlers/jobs.py: run_job
- workers/queue.py: consume
Flag a catch-all anywhere else.

trace.text: Skips the three listed functions correctly.
PR #610 adds handlers/webhooks.py with the same logging catch-all.
Not on the list: flags it as a swallowed exception.
Developer dismisses it and asks who maintains the list.

options.verdict: Works for listed files, fails on the next new one.
options.why: More detailed prose is what already failed, and a hard-coded list does not generalise to new handlers. Contrastive examples teach the pattern instead.

options.text: Add two or three contrastive examples: a logging top-level handler marked acceptable and a swallowed exception marked as an issue.
options.code:
<example verdict="acceptable">
handlers/api.py: except Exception -> log, 500
Why: top-level boundary; error is logged
and surfaced to the caller.
</example>
<example verdict="flag">
billing/charge.py: except Exception: pass
Why: failure hidden; caller thinks it worked.
</example>

trace.text: PR #610 adds handlers/webhooks.py with a logging catch-all.
Matches the acceptable example: boundary handler, logged. Skips it.
Flags "except: pass" in refunds/sync.py, citing the hidden failure.
Dismissal rate falls from 40% to 8% over two weeks.

options.verdict: Real catches kept, deliberate handlers left alone.
options.why: Examples that separate acceptable patterns from genuine issues show the decision boundary and generalise to new files. Prose had already failed to do that.

labs.takeaway: False positives on deliberate patterns → contrastive examples showing both sides and the reason.

labs.title: Agent starts with the wrong lookup tool
labs.context: Your support agent has get_customer and lookup_order, and their descriptions were rewritten last month and are clear. For ambiguous messages such as "I was charged twice", the agent starts with get_customer on some runs and lookup_order on others, and a wrong start adds two extra turns. scenario.title: Structured Data Extraction
scenario.story:
A research-analytics team built a pipeline that pulls `sample_size` and `citations` from academic papers. It worked well on journal articles. Then they added 50 conference papers, and 80% came back with both fields null.

The first fix was more instructions: "sample size may appear anywhere, look very carefully, never leave required fields empty". The null rate barely moved, and nine papers now had a sample size of 100 that appeared nowhere in the text.

An engineer read the failures. The conference papers had no Methods heading. They gave the sample as "(n=312)" in the introduction and cited work inline as "[Lee 2021]". Every example in the prompt was a journal paper.

She removed the "never leave empty" line and wrote three short examples: a journal paper, a conference paper with inline details, and a position paper where `sample_size` is correctly null. On the next run the null rate fell to 6%, and every remaining null was a paper with no study in it.

plain: If you need Claude to return data in a fixed shape, describe that shape as a tool with a JSON schema and have Claude call the tool. A JSON schema is a description of which fields exist and what type each one is. This removes broken JSON, but it does not guarantee the values are right. Field design and `tool_choice` decide how far you can trust the values.
analogy: A paper form with labelled boxes stops people writing a free-form letter, but it cannot stop them writing the wrong number in the "total" box.
currentNote: On Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5.1, forced `tool_choice` (`any` or `tool`) returns HTTP 400, and with manual extended thinking it errors on every model. For guaranteed structure on current models, use `tool_choice: auto` with `"strict": true` on the tool, or structured outputs via `output_config.format` with a `json_schema`, and still check `stop_reason`.

sections.body:
**Define a tool with a JSON schema, and Claude's answer arrives as structured data instead of free text.**

A tool has a `name`, a `description` and an `input_schema`: a JSON schema listing the fields and their types. When Claude calls the tool, the response contains a `tool_use` block whose `input` is an object in that shape. Your code reads the fields directly.

For extraction, the "tool" often does nothing at all. `extract_invoice` exists only so Claude fills in its fields.

Why bother? If you ask for "JSON in your reply", Claude usually complies, but sometimes it adds "Here is the JSON:" or a trailing comma, and `json.loads` fails on document 37 of 500. Tool use with a schema eliminates those **syntax errors**. It is the most reliable route to schema-compliant output.

**`auto` may reply in text, `any` must call some tool, and a forced tool must call the named one.**

The `tool_choice` parameter controls whether Claude has to call a tool:

- `{"type": "auto"}`: Claude may call a tool **or answer in text**. Fine for chat, risky in a pipeline that expects a `tool_use` block.
- `{"type": "any"}`: Claude **must call one of the tools** and chooses which. Use it when you have several schemas (invoice, receipt, contract) and do not know the document type.
- `{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}`: Claude **must call that tool**. Use it when one step must run first, such as metadata before enrichment.

**In current models:** forced choices (`any`, `tool`) return HTTP 400 on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Fable 5.1. There you use `auto` with `"strict": true` on the tool, or `output_config.format` with a JSON schema. Exam questions still expect the choices above.

**Good schemas make the honest answer easy: nullable fields, `"unclear"` and `"other"`.**

A schema fixes the shape. Its design decides whether Claude can be honest:

- **Nullable fields.** If an invoice may lack a due date, use `"type": ["string", "null"]`. If the field must be a string, Claude is pushed to invent one, such as "2024-01-01".
- **`"unclear"` in enums.** When a currency symbol is smudged, Claude can say so instead of guessing `"USD"`.
- **`"other"` plus a detail string.** A `currency` enum of GBP, EUR, USD and `"other"`, with `currency_detail` holding "CHF", captures new values without a schema change.
- **Normalisation rules in the prompt.** If sources write dates as "3rd March" and "03/03/25", add "dates as YYYY-MM-DD" to the prompt and the field description. The schema fixes the type; the rule fixes the format.

**A schema-valid answer can still be wrong, so check the values too.**

Tool use guarantees structure, not truth. All of these pass the schema:

- line items that add up to £940 while `stated_total` says £1,040;
- a supplier's VAT number placed in `invoice_number`;
- a date in the right format but taken from the wrong line.

These are **semantic errors**, and a schema cannot see them. Catch them with checks in your code, such as comparing a `calculated_total` with the `stated_total` (lesson 4.4).

Exam habit: split the problem in the stem. Parse failures and malformed JSON point to tool use with a schema. Wrong or invented values point to schema design or validation. If the source can lack the value, the answer is a nullable field, not a stricter schema.

scenario.title: Structured Data Extraction
scenario.story:
An accounts-payable team had a shared inbox of unlabelled PDFs: invoices, receipts and the odd contract. Their first version asked Claude to "return the fields as JSON" and parsed the reply. On a run of 500 documents, 11 failed to parse, and field names drifted between `due_date` and `dueDate`.

They moved to three extraction tools with JSON schemas. Parse errors stopped, but two new problems appeared. With `tool_choice` set to `auto`, a scanned letter got a text reply and was silently dropped. And because `due_date` had to be a string, invoices with no due date came back with invented dates. Finance chased a payment that was never due.

The fix was in the design. They set `tool_choice` to `any` so every document produced a tool call, made `due_date` nullable and added `"unclear"` to the currency enum. Nulls and unclear values went to a review queue. When they later moved to Sonnet 5.5, forced choices returned 400, so they switched to structured outputs with `output_config.format`.

plain: After Claude extracts data, your code checks it. If a check fails, you can send it back with the error and ask for a fix. That works when Claude made a mistake, but not when the information is simply not in the document. Good fields also let you spot conflicts in the source and learn which findings people keep rejecting.
analogy: A teacher can hand back a maths test saying "question 3: your sum is wrong", and the student can fix it. No amount of handing back will help if the question needed a table that was never in the exam paper.

sections.body:
**Check every output in code, retry with targeted feedback, and route what cannot be fixed.**

A validation loop has three steps:

1. **Validate.** Your code checks the output. Does it match the schema? Is `due_date` in YYYY-MM-DD? Do the line items add up?
2. **Retry with error feedback.** If a check fails, send a new request with the **original document**, the **failed extraction** and the **specific validation errors**, such as "due_date '3rd March' is not YYYY-MM-DD".
3. **Accept or route.** If it passes, keep it. If it still fails after a capped number of retries (two is common), flag it for a person.

All three parts of the feedback matter. Claude re-reads the document, sees exactly what it wrote, and corrects only what is wrong. "Validation failed, try again" gives it nothing to work from.

**Retries fix format and structure; they cannot create information the source does not contain.**

Before retrying, ask one question: **is the correct value in the document I sent?**

- **Yes.** Retries work well: a date in the wrong format, an amount in pence instead of pounds, a field left out that is plainly on the page. One targeted retry usually fixes these.
- **No.** Retries are pointless. If the PO number appears only on a separate purchase order that was never sent, "try harder" cannot find it. Claude can only guess, and a guessed PO number that passes validation is worse than a null.

For absent values, set the field to null and flag it, or route the record to someone who has the other document. Sort errors into these two groups in code, so you retry only the first group.

**Some fields exist only to make semantic errors and messy sources visible.**

A schema cannot tell you that numbers disagree. Extra fields can:

- **`calculated_total` next to `stated_total`.** Claude adds up the line items itself and also copies the printed total. If £940 sits next to £1,040, your validator catches it.
- **`conflict_detected`.** A boolean Claude sets when the source contradicts itself, for example two different totals on one invoice. It reports both instead of quietly picking one. Forcing reconciliation hides a problem a person should see.
- **`detected_pattern` on review findings.** Each finding records the pattern it matched, such as "broad-except". Later you can count which patterns developers dismiss as false positives and tighten those criteria (lesson 4.1).

**The usual failures are blind retries, thin feedback, forced answers and loosened schemas.**

- **"Try harder" for absent data.** It costs calls and invites fabrication. Check the source first.
- **Error-only feedback.** Without the document and the previous output, Claude rebuilds the record from scratch and may make new mistakes.
- **Asking Claude to reconcile** conflicting totals into one number. Use `conflict_detected` and let a person decide.
- **Loosening the schema** so the date check stops failing. "3rd March" then flows into the payments system, which cannot parse it, and the supplier is paid late.
- **Unbounded retries.** Cap them. A stubborn error should end in a review queue, not a loop.

Exam habit: check whether the missing or wrong value exists in the provided source. That decides whether retrying can help.

labs.title: Dismissals jump but nobody knows which findings
labs.context: After a model upgrade, the share of CI review findings that developers dismiss rose from 12% to 35%. Each finding carries only a file, a line and a free-text message, so dismissals cannot be grouped by kind. The team wants to find which kinds of finding are now being dismissed so it can rewrite those criteria.
labs.question: What change best enables that analysis?

options.text: Add a confidence score to each finding and suppress findings that score below 0.7 before they are posted.

trace.text: Suppresses 22% of findings, including 9 real bugs.
Dismissal rate falls to 29%.
Team still cannot say which kinds of finding are dismissed.

options.verdict: Fewer posts, no insight.
options.why: Right pattern, wrong problem: it filters output but answers nothing about which kinds are dismissed. Confidence filtering also drops real bugs.

options.text: Ask developers to choose a dismissal reason from a short dropdown whenever they dismiss a finding.
options.code:
dismiss_reasons:
  - not_a_bug
  - not_useful
  - already_known
  - other

trace.text: Developers pick "not_useful" for 70% of dismissals.
Reasons say why it was rejected, not what the bot detected.
Team still cannot map dismissals to review criteria.

options.verdict: Data on feelings, not on patterns.
options.why: Dismissal reasons describe the developer's reaction, not which pattern the reviewer flagged. Without a pattern label on the finding, nothing can be grouped by criteria.

options.text: Add a detected_pattern field to each finding, such as "unchecked-null-return", then group dismissals by that pattern.

One week: 1,140 findings, 400 dismissed.
Grouping shows "missing-docstring" is 61% of dismissals.
Team rewrites that one criterion; dismissals fall to 14%.

options.why: A detected_pattern field makes each finding's pattern explicit, so dismissals can be analysed by kind. That points straight at the criteria to rewrite.

Rephrases the same finding more cautiously.
Re-posts it on the PR; developer dismisses it again.

options.verdict: Same finding, reworded, dismissed twice.
options.why: Right pattern, wrong problem: retry-with-feedback fixes validation errors, and a dismissal is not one. It also gives the team no grouped data.

labs.takeaway: To learn which findings developers dismiss, give each finding a detected_pattern field.

labs.title: Synthesis averages two conflicting market figures

Report subagent writes: "Estimates range from $4.1bn [S3] to $6.3bn [S7]."

options.code:
Synthesis rules:
- Output one value per metric.
- When sources disagree on a figure, use the
  value from the most recently published source.

Report states $6.3bn [S7] only.

scenario.title: Structured Data Extraction
scenario.story:
A logistics firm extracts invoices into its payments system. Validation started failing on about 5% of records, so an engineer added a quick fix: on any failure, call Claude again with "Validation failed. Try harder and make sure every field is filled in."

Failures dropped to almost zero. A month later an auditor found purchase-order numbers in the ledger that matched no real order. The PO number usually lives on a separate purchase order, which the pipeline never sent. The retry had pushed Claude to invent one, and the validator, which only checked the format, accepted it.

The team rebuilt the loop. The validator now labels each error as either a format problem or "absent in source". Format problems, such as "3rd March" for a due date, get one retry that includes the original invoice, the failed extraction and the exact error. Absent values stay null and go to the accounts team. They also added `calculated_total` and `conflict_detected`, which caught three invoices with mismatched totals in the first week.

plain: The Message Batches API lets you send many requests at once and collect the answers later, at half the normal price. The catch is that results can take up to 24 hours and there is no promise of speed. It suits work nobody is waiting on, not work that blocks a person or a merge.
analogy: It is like posting a parcel by the cheap, slow service. Fine for a birthday present sent weeks early; useless for the contract that must be signed today.
currentNote: A batch request can include tool definitions and earlier conversation turns, including past tool results. What it cannot do is complete a client-side tool round trip inside the batch: each turn that needs your tool's result must be another request or batch. Most batches finish within an hour, but 24 hours is the only guarantee.

sections.body:
**The Message Batches API halves the cost in exchange for slower, unguaranteed turnaround.**

A batch is a list of ordinary Messages requests submitted in one go. They are processed in the background and you collect the results later.

Key facts:

- **50% cheaper** than the same requests sent synchronously.
- **Up to 24 hours** to process. Most batches finish within an hour, but there is **no latency SLA**, meaning no promise of speed. Requests still unfinished at 24 hours expire.
- Each request carries a **`custom_id`** (1 to 64 letters, digits, `-` or `_`) that you use to match its result.
- Each result has a type: `succeeded`, `errored`, `canceled` or `expired`.

Think of it as posting letters instead of making phone calls. It is cheaper, but you cannot stand at the counter waiting for the reply.

sections.h: How it works, step by step
sections.body:
**Test on a sample, submit with unique IDs, match results by `custom_id`, and resubmit only the failures.**

1. **Refine the prompt on a sample** of, say, 50 documents with the normal API. Finding a prompt bug after 10,000 items is expensive.
2. **Build the requests.** Each has a unique `custom_id` such as `"doc-00417"` and the usual `params`: model, max_tokens, messages.
3. **Submit** the batch and poll until `processing_status` is `"ended"`.
4. **Read the results by `custom_id`.** They can come back in any order, so never pair them with requests by position.
5. **Handle failures item by item.** Save `succeeded` results. For the rest, fix the cause, for example by chunking an oversized document, and resubmit **only those** items.

Rerunning the whole batch pays again for everything that already worked, and unfixed items simply fail again.

sections.h: When to use batch and when not to
sections.body:
**If someone is waiting, or the job needs a tool round trip, use the synchronous API.**

Ask two questions:

- **Does a person or a merge wait on the result?** A pre-merge check blocks a developer, so it stays synchronous. Overnight reports, weekly audits and nightly test generation can wait, so they suit batch.
- **Does the job need your tool's result mid-request?** A batch request can include tools and earlier turns, but it cannot call your tool, receive the result and carry on inside the batch. An agent that searches, reads and searches again would need a new request or batch for every turn. In exam terms: no multi-turn tool calling within a request.

"Batches usually finish quickly" is not a reason to batch blocking work. Usually is not a guarantee, and one slow batch can hold up merges for a day.

**Plan deadlines on the full 24 hours, not on how fast batches usually are.**

Suppose you promise results within **30 hours** of a document arriving. Processing can take up to 24 hours, which leaves 6 hours for waiting before submission.

If you submit the accumulated documents every **4 hours**:

- a document that arrives just after a submission waits up to 4 hours;
- it then takes up to 24 hours to process;
- worst case: 28 hours, inside the 30-hour promise.

Submitting once a day would break the promise, because a document could wait nearly 24 hours before it is even sent.

When not to plan this way: if the deadline is shorter than 24 hours, batch cannot guarantee it at all, so use the synchronous API.

items: Agent loops with tool round trips

right.title: Message Batches API

example.title: Worked example: nightly batch with resubmit-by-id
example.code:
requests = [
    {"custom_id": f"doc-{d.id}",
     "params": {"model": MODEL, "max_tokens": 2048,
                "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": d.text}]}}
    for d in tonight_docs
]
batch = client.messages.batches.create(requests=requests)

# later, once batches.retrieve(batch.id).processing_status == "ended"
failed = []
for r in client.messages.batches.results(batch.id):
    if r.result.type == "succeeded":
        save(r.custom_id, r.result.message.content)
    else:  # errored, expired or canceled
        failed.append(r.custom_id)

retry = [fix_request(cid) for cid in failed]  # e.g. chunk big docs
if retry:
    client.messages.batches.create(requests=retry)
notes: Every request gets a unique `custom_id` built from the document id.
Results are saved by `custom_id`, never by position in the output.
Each result has a type; only `succeeded` items are saved.
Only the failed ids are rebuilt with a fix and resubmitted, not the whole batch.
This is a nightly job, so the up-to-24-hour window is acceptable even though most batches finish within an hour.

labs.title: Finance wants batch savings on CI jobs
labs.context: Your CI runs two Claude jobs: a pre-merge check that developers wait on before merging, and a nightly job that generates tests for about 600 modules. Finance wants the 50% Message Batches saving wherever it is safe. Last night's trial batch had six failures caused by oversized modules.
labs.question: Which plan best meets these goals?

options.text: Move both jobs to the Message Batches API, since most batches finish well within an hour.

Pre-merge request submitted as a batch.
Batch queue is busy; status stays "in_progress".
14:30 PR is still blocked. Developer pings the platform team.

options.why: Batch has no latency SLA and can take up to 24 hours. A workflow that blocks a person or a merge must stay synchronous.

options.text: Batch the nightly job, match results to requests by their position in the output, and rerun the whole batch if any request fails.

22:00 Nightly batch of 600 test-generation requests submitted.

options.why: Someone waiting means synchronous; work that can wait suits batch. Failures are resubmitted by custom_id with a fix.

Trimmed prompts cut cost by about 15%.

labs.title: Huge backfill with an untested prompt
labs.context: You must extract key terms from 80,000 archived supplier contracts with the Message Batches API, and results are due in two weeks. The prompt is new and has been tried on only five hand-picked contracts. Last year a similar full run had to be repeated because a prompt flaw affected most records.
labs.question: How should the team run this job?

options.text: Submit all 80,000 contracts now, then resubmit any failed requests by custom_id with a fix once the batch has ended.

trace.text: Batch ends: 79,880 succeeded, 120 errored.
120 errored requests chunked and resubmitted by custom_id.
Audit: renewal_date holds the signature date on 60% of contracts.
Those requests "succeeded", so the whole job must be rerun.

options.why: Resubmitting by custom_id fixes errored requests, not a prompt flaw in succeeded ones. The untested prompt is the real risk.

options.text: Run the whole job on the synchronous API so prompt problems show up at once and can be fixed mid-run.

  --input contracts/ \

options.text: Split the contracts into ten batches of 8,000 and submit them all at once so the work finishes sooner.

for i in $(seq 0 9); do
  python submit_batch.py --shard $i --of 10
done

All ten end within 6 hours.
Audit: the same renewal_date flaw in every shard.

# 2. review results, fix prompt, rerun sample

python submit_batch.py --all --prompt v3

scenario.title: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
scenario.story:
A platform team ran two Claude jobs in CI: a pre-merge code check and a nightly job that generated unit tests for 600 modules. Finance asked them to move both to the Message Batches API for the 50% saving.

They tried it for a week. The nightly job was fine. The pre-merge check was not. Most batches came back within an hour, but on Wednesday one sat "in_progress" from 09:05 until 23:10, and three developers lost a day waiting to merge.

The team split the work. Pre-merge checks went back to the synchronous API, because a person waits on them. The nightly job stayed on batch, with each request's `custom_id` set to `test-<module>`.

The next morning the batch reported 594 succeeded and 6 errored, all very large modules. Their first script paired results with requests by position and saved tests under the wrong file names. They rewrote it to key everything by `custom_id`, chunked the six large modules and resubmitted only those. The nightly bill fell by about half.

plain: Claude is better at finding problems in work it did not write. A separate review run, with a fresh context, catches more than asking the same session to check itself. For big changes, review each file on its own and then do one extra pass that looks at how the files fit together.
analogy: Authors miss their own typos because they read what they meant to write. A second person reading cold spots them. And an editor checks each chapter, then reads the whole book once for plot holes between chapters.

sections.body:
**Have someone other than the author review the work, and review big changes in focused passes.**

Two patterns that work together:

- **Multi-instance review.** The **generator** is the Claude session that wrote the code or extraction. The **reviewer** is a separate, **independent instance**: a new session with a fresh context that sees the output and the requirements, but not the generator's reasoning.
- **Multi-pass review.** A large change is split into **per-file passes** for local bugs, plus one **cross-file integration pass** for problems between files.

Both reduce missed issues, contradictory findings and **self-confirmation bias**, the tendency to approve your own reasoning. Human teams work the same way: authors do not approve their own pull requests.

**A generator re-reads its own reasoning and tends to agree with it.**

The session that wrote the code still holds its plan in context, for example "rename `user_id` everywhere and update callers". Asked to review, it checks the files against that plan, finds they match, and reports "no issues". It does not ask whether the plan missed a caller.

These do **not** fix it:

- "Now critically review the code you just wrote."
- Turning on **extended thinking** for the generator. More thinking in the same context is still the same point of view.
- Passing the generator's reasoning to the reviewer "so it understands the intent". That carries the bias across.

What fixes it: start a new instance with a fresh `messages` list, give it the diff and the requirements, and ask it to find bugs.

**Per-file passes catch local bugs; a separate integration pass catches what breaks between files.**

One pass over a 15-file, 4,000-line diff spreads attention thin. Claude may find bugs in the first few files and miss file 14. It can also contradict itself, calling a line correct early on and flagging it later.

A better structure:

1. **Per-file passes.** One focused review per file, looking only for local bugs.
2. **Integration pass.** One review that looks only at cross-file concerns: renamed fields, changed function signatures, call sites, shared types and config.

Do not drop the integration pass. Per-file passes cannot see that `models.py` renamed a field which `reports/export.py` still reads. That breakage only shows up when you look across files.

For a small one-file change, a single independent pass is enough.

**Ask the reviewer for a confidence rating on each finding, then send each finding to the right place.**

Human review time is limited. A **verification pass**, in which the reviewer rates its confidence in each finding, lets you route them:

- **High-confidence** findings post straight to the pull request.
- **Medium or low** findings go to a human queue for a quick check.

This is routing, not filtering. Nothing is silently dropped; each finding goes where it can be handled best. It works best when the review criteria are already explicit (lesson 4.1), so a rating means something specific.

What goes wrong: using one confidence threshold to hide findings, which loses real bugs; or routing the generator's own self-review, which still carries its bias.

steps.label: Route by confidence
steps.note: High to PR, others to humans

example.title: Worked example: independent per-file and integration passes
example.code:
REVIEW_SYSTEM = "You review code you did not write. Report bugs only."

def review(prompt):
    # fresh messages list: no generator history or reasoning
    return client.messages.create(
        model=MODEL, max_tokens=4096, system=REVIEW_SYSTEM,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
    )

findings = []
for f in changed_files:  # pass 1: local issues, one file at a time
    findings += parse(review(f"Review {f.path}:\n{f.diff}"))

summary = "\n".join(f"{f.path}: {f.signature_changes}" for f in changed_files)
findings += parse(review(  # pass 2: cross-file integration
    "Check only cross-file issues: callers, signatures, shared types.\n"
    + summary + "\n" + all_call_sites(changed_files)
))

for f in findings:  # route by per-finding confidence
    (post_to_pr if f.confidence == "high" else human_queue)(f)
notes: Each `review()` call starts a new messages list, so the reviewer never sees the generator's reasoning.
Pass 1 runs once per file, so attention is not diluted across the whole change.
Pass 2 is the integration pass and only looks at cross-file concerns.
Each finding carries a confidence value used to route it, not to drop it.

labs.title: Two pharmacists cannot check 6,000 records
labs.context: Your pipeline extracts drug name, dose and frequency from 6,000 handwritten prescription scans a day, and two pharmacists can check about 300 records. They check a random 300, which are almost always correct, while audits show errors cluster in hard-to-read scans. Every record must still flow downstream the same day.
labs.question: How should the team choose which records the pharmacists check?

options.text: Add a verification pass that reports confidence for each field, and route the lowest-confidence records to the pharmacists.

trace.text: Verifier re-reads each scan against the extraction, field by field.
rx-20931: dose "50mg" low confidence, "could be 500mg".
280 low-confidence records go to the pharmacists; the rest flow on.
Pharmacists correct 61 errors in a day, up from 3.

options.verdict: Reviewer time goes where the errors are.
options.why: A verification pass with per-field confidence enables calibrated routing. Limited reviewer capacity goes to the records most likely to be wrong.

options.text: Have the extraction call itself add a confidence score to each field, and route low-scoring records for review.

trace.text: Reads "50mg" on a smudged scan; rates it 0.93.
Only 40 records score low; most smudged scans pass.
A tenfold dosing error reaches the pharmacy system.

options.text: Run every scan through extraction twice and send the pharmacists only the records where the two outputs differ.

  runs: 2            # same model, same prompt
  review_if: outputs_differ
  otherwise: accept

Both runs misread the same smudged "500" as "50".
Outputs agree, so the error is not routed.

options.verdict: Double the cost; shared misreads slip through.
options.why: Over-engineered, and two identical passes share the same blind spots. Per-field confidence from a verification pass targets doubt directly.

return null for it.

scenario.title: Claude Code for Continuous Integration
scenario.story:
A team used Claude Code to rename `user_id` to `account_id` across a 15-file service. Before merging, the developer typed into the same session: "Now critically review everything you just wrote. Think hard." Claude checked each file against its own plan and reported no issues.

CI disagreed. An integration test failed with a `KeyError`: `reports/export.py` still read `row["user_id"]`.

The developer tried again with a fresh session and pasted all 15 diffs, about 4,000 lines. This reviewer found two local bugs but missed the export file, and described one line in `models.py` as both correct and inconsistent.

The team then set up their CI review properly. A new reviewer instance, with no generator history, runs one pass per changed file for local bugs. A final integration pass looks only at renamed fields, signatures and call sites. Each finding carries a confidence rating: high ones post to the pull request, the rest go to a human queue. On the next refactor, the integration pass flagged a stale field before anyone merged.
